## Cards

### 01 · Children, and the people raising them
Group: **Growing up** · Referral chip: **Ask your care team** · Products shown: *none*

**The one that matters most** `1.s1`

- A small body has very little fluid in reserve, so a child — especially a baby with an ileostomy — can get dehydrated far faster than an adult losing the same amount. Steady salt loss can also show up as poor weight gain long before anything looks like dehydration, which is why your team may weigh your baby often `1.s1.1`
- Ask what your child’s normal output is and what counts as too much for their size. Call the same day for output that suddenly rises or turns watery, fewer wet diapers, no tears, a sunken soft spot, unusual sleepiness, or weight that stalls or drops — that is a call to your team, not something to manage with extra fluids at home `1.s1.2`

**Products and skin** `1.s2`

- A child’s stoma is not a smaller version of an adult one. They grow, so sizes change constantly — re-measuring is routine rather than occasional `1.s2.1`
- Pediatric products are a real category rather than repackaged adult stock, shaped smaller and more flexibly for a small abdomen. The adhesive is the part that gets overstated: it is largely the same material as the adult ranges. A baby born at term starts with skin barrier function much like an adult’s, so the extra caution about fragile skin is really for babies born early or at low birth weight, and children who are unwell `1.s2.2`
- When a pouch keeps lifting, the answer is usually to change it more often rather than to make it stick harder — pediatric barriers are thinner, so they hold up to output for less time. Adhesive removers, barrier films, skin cement and benzoin are generally avoided in infants and young children, because more of any chemical is absorbed through their skin and a stronger bond can tear it on removal. A seal that keeps failing is a call to your child’s ostomy nurse, not a trip for stronger products `1.s2.3`

**Two things worth knowing before they happen** `1.s3`

- A child’s stoma can prolapse — telescope outward and look alarmingly long. It is more common in children than in adults and usually not an emergency, but colour matters more than length: a stoma that darkens or goes dusky needs an emergency department rather than a phone call, and so does pain, or output that stops ✎ `1.s3.1`
- In a child with an ileostomy, high-fibre foods can cause a blockage, so new foods go in one at a time. Ask your team what each of these looks like for your child, and which number to call after hours `1.s3.2`

**School, and afterwards** `1.s4`

- School needs a written plan rather than a conversation in September: who knows and who backs them up on days they are away, where a spare kit and a full change of clothes live, private washroom access without having to ask in front of the class, and a number the school can call `1.s4.1`
- Most Canadian schools have no nurse on site, so ask who owns the plan — usually the principal, sometimes a public health nurse — and make sure supply teachers get it. Most schools have never been asked before, so expect to be the one explaining `1.s4.2`
- Ask the children’s hospital about transition planning a year or two before it happens, and about who the adult service will be. The handoff around seventeen or eighteen is the point at which families most often fall out of specialist care altogether, and it goes better when it is arranged rather than arrived at `1.s4.3`

> **Note** `1.note` — Pediatric ostomy care belongs with a children’s hospital team — the service that created the stoma, working with a nurse who practises in pediatrics. One practical note: “pediatric NSWOC” describes where a nurse works rather than a credential you can search for, and the NSWOCC directory filters by city and by wound, ostomy or continence, with no pediatric option. So the hospital team is the first call, and the one who can point you to the right nurse near you. Coverage for children differs from the adult rules — see Funding & Coverage.

### 02 · Being in your twenties with one
Group: **Growing up** · Referral chip: **Ask someone who has one** · Products shown: *none*

**Telling people** `2.s1`

- There is no rule about when to tell a partner, and no version of it you owe anyone. Some people say it early so it is out of the way; others wait until someone knows them a bit first `2.s1.1`
- It often goes fine. It sometimes does not — and if someone decides they cannot be with you because of your stoma, that is information about them rather than a sign you handled it wrong `2.s1.2`
- Practise it once out loud, with a friend or a peer visitor, before it matters. It is easier the second time `2.s1.3`

**Studying and going out** `2.s2`

- University accommodations are real and not a favour, but they usually run through two offices: exam arrangements through accessibility services, residence through campus housing, on a separate application. Both want documentation from your care team and both have deadlines that can fall months before term, so ask early — and what is on offer varies, since a private washroom is not something every campus provides `2.s2.1`
- Alcohol changes output for a lot of people, but the bigger issue is fluid. It is a diuretic, and with an ileostomy you are already losing more water and salt than you used to — dehydration is the most common reason people end up back in hospital after ileostomy surgery. A long night out is still worth planning around rather than avoiding, and if your output is already high, ask your NSWOC or dietitian what your fluid plan should look like first `2.s2.2`
- Ostomy Canada runs Gutsy Gang social clubs for roughly the 20 to 40 age group, in several cities. Some chapters run the same group under another name, so it is worth asking locally rather than searching only for that one `2.s2.3`

> **Note** `2.s2.note` — Being the only person you know with one is the hardest part for most people this age, and it is the part a peer group fixes fastest.

### 03 · Pregnancy and becoming a parent
Group: **Bodies that change** · Referral chip: **Ask your gastroenterologist** · Products shown: *none*

**Before you try** `3.s1`

- If your ostomy is because of IBD, the biggest thing you can influence is where your disease sits when you conceive. Going in while it is quiet is associated with outcomes close to anyone else’s, and conceiving during a flare makes preterm birth and low birth weight more likely `3.s1.1`
- Start that conversation with your gastroenterologist before you start trying to conceive, rather than after. Some medication decisions take months to settle, and stopping treatment on your own is the thing most likely to go wrong `3.s1.2`
- Getting pregnant may take longer if you have had pelvic surgery. Pouch surgery in particular is linked to reduced fertility — people with a pelvic pouch are around three times more likely to use IVF — though once they do, their chance of a live birth is the same as anyone else’s. Worth raising early, so that a slow start does not read as an answer `3.s1.3`

**While you are pregnant** `3.s2`

- People with ostomies do have healthy pregnancies, and a stoma is not a reason not to. It does mean being followed more closely than usual: stoma problems in pregnancy are common rather than rare — blockage and a drop in output are the ones that come up most, and prolapse and parastomal hernia are also reported — and preterm birth is somewhat more likely. Almost all of it is manageable when your team knows to watch for it `3.s2.1`
- Your abdomen changes shape substantially, so the stoma does too — expect to re-measure often and to change products more than once along the way `3.s2.2`
- Settle one thing in advance: what counts as an emergency. Blockage is the most common stoma problem in pregnancy, so ask your surgeon or NSWOC now what should make you phone or come in. Get your own threshold and your own number before you need them `3.s2.3`

> **Note** `3.s2.note` — Most of what is known here comes from bowel stomas, so if you have a urostomy or ileal conduit, ask your urologist what is different for you.

**Delivery** `3.s3`

- How you deliver is a discussion between you, your obstetric team, your surgical team, and — if your ostomy is because of IBD — your gastroenterologist. Having a stoma does not decide it on its own, but some histories do push toward a planned caesarean, and in practice caesarean rates in people with a stoma run well above average. Ask early which of that applies to you `3.s3.1`
- If you have an ileal pouch or a continent diversion, say so explicitly. A pouch is not a stoma, and guidelines lean toward a planned caesarean after pouch surgery to protect the sphincter and the pouch’s long-term function. The evidence behind that is not strong and teams do disagree, which is exactly why it belongs in a conversation months ahead rather than one in labour `3.s3.2`

**Afterwards** `3.s4`

- The stoma usually settles back toward its pre-pregnancy size over the following weeks, so there is another round of re-measuring and probably another product change on the far side `3.s4.1`
- Ask about lifting before you are home with a toddler to pick up. Parastomal hernia is the risk being managed, and the advice is specific to your surgery rather than general `3.s4.2`
- Medication while breastfeeding is a gastroenterologist question if your ostomy is because of IBD. Stopping treatment unilaterally is the common mistake, and it is a phone call to avoid it `3.s4.3`

> **Note** `3.note` — If you are planning a pregnancy, start before you conceive — your gastroenterologist or surgeon, and an NSWOC. If you are already pregnant, tell your obstetric team about your ostomy at the first appointment and ask for an NSWOC to be involved early rather than when something goes wrong.

### 04 · Later life, and managing more than one thing
Group: **Bodies that change** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**What tends to get harder** `4.s1`

- Dexterity and eyesight. Moldable barriers you shape with your fingers instead of cutting, larger tabs and simpler closures all exist for exactly this. Pre-cut works if your stoma is round and its size has settled; one-piece has fewer steps, while two-piece can be easier to line up by feel. There is no single right answer, so ask an NSWOC to trial a few with you rather than struggling with what you have `4.s1.1`
- Skin gets thinner and tears more easily with age, and it usually shows up on removal — peel low and slow, pressing the skin away from the barrier rather than pulling the barrier off. Fit still matters just as much, because a barrier that leaks puts output onto skin that is slower to recover. Worth having an NSWOC watch you do a full change `4.s1.2`
- Managing several conditions at once means more medication, and how much of a pill you absorb depends on your ostomy: with an ileostomy, extended-release and enteric-coated forms can pass through before they have finished working, while a colostomy is closer to normal. Ask a pharmacist to go through the whole list, including anything you buy over the counter `4.s1.3`

**What is worth arranging** `4.s2`

- Home care and community nursing can help with changes — ask your care team what your province provides rather than assuming there is nothing. Most provinces also fund a pharmacist medication review, and in some, including Ontario, a pharmacist can come to you `4.s2.1`
- If someone helps you, have them taught by an NSWOC directly — doing a change themselves with the nurse there, not just watching one. Book again if your stoma, your skin, or your products change `4.s2.2`
- If a move to a retirement residence or long-term care is coming, raise the ostomy before the move rather than after. Staff frequently have no ostomy experience, and the route your supplies arrive by usually changes with the address `4.s2.3`

> **Note** `4.s2.note` — Several provincial programs cover more for seniors, and some are seniors-only — see Funding & Coverage.

### 05 · If you are the one helping
Group: **The people around it** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Ask what kind of help is wanted before offering it. Plenty of people want company and logistics, not hands-on care, and being asked is better than being managed `5.1`
- If you are doing hands-on care, ask an NSWOC to teach you directly — secondhand instructions are how skin problems start `5.2`
- Caring for someone is tiring in a way people underestimate. Most support groups welcome family and partners, and that is not an imposition on the group `5.3`

### 06 · Where to bring the weight of it
Group: **The people around it** · Referral chip: **Call, do not wait** *(warning tone — do not act on this page alone)* · Products shown: *none*

- Ostomy Canada’s Visitor Program puts you in touch with a trained peer visitor who has one themselves. It is support in its own right, not only a way to rehearse a difficult conversation, and it is free `6.1`
- A local chapter or peer support group is the other standing door, and several run online rather than only in person — worth knowing if you are rural, newly post-operative, or not ready to walk into a room. Listings do go stale, so if the one near you looks dead, Ostomy Canada’s national line is 1-888-969-9698 `6.2`
- Low mood and anxiety are common after ostomy surgery, and they tend to rise in the months afterwards rather than settle. If it is not lifting, that is a reason to say so to your family doctor or surgical team — there is no ostomy-specific counselling service in Canada, so the route runs through your usual primary care and your province’s mental health services `6.3`

> **Note** `6.note` — Nothing here is a substitute for urgent help. If you are thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time.

- **Later life** `band.3` — Your NSWOC for fit as dexterity changes, a pharmacist for a full medication review, and your province’s home care program.

## Pharmacist panel

- **eyebrow** `pharmacist.eyebrow` — Available in Ontario
- **heading** `pharmacist.heading` — Product and restock questions, whoever you are
- **body** `pharmacist.body` — An Ontario pharmacist can help with what products exist in smaller sizes, what is easier to handle, and how a medication list looks alongside an ostomy — during business hours until 5 p.m. Eastern. Anything about a child, a pregnancy, or a change in someone’s ability to manage belongs with an NSWOC or the treating team.
- **cta** `pharmacist.cta` — Talk to a Pharmacist

## Closing

**Most of this is a conversation, not an article** `closing.heading`

The four situations here are the ones where general advice runs out fastest. Knowing that, and knowing who to ask, is genuinely most of the work. `closing.body`

## Disclaimer

This is general information, not medical advice. Care for children, during pregnancy, and for people managing several conditions differs in ways this page does not attempt to cover — it is here to tell you what changes and who to ask. Speak to an NSWOC and the treating team rather than relying on general ostomy guidance, including ours. `disclaimer`
